If you're like me, you are paying for a ton of subscriptions you don't even remember signing up for. Let's make this the year of only having subscriptions that add to our lives. The digital services below are the best things you can 

While there's no single digital service that everyone will like, Apple One comes close. Anyone with an iPhone (i.e., most phone users in the U.S.) will appreciate a single digital bundle that covers Apple Music, Apple TV+, Arcade, and extra iCloud storage. That's streaming, gaming, and storage covered for $21.95 a month. Pro tip: The Family Plan includes six separate accounts for $27.95 a month, and your "family" could include anyone, so get some friends together to get the most out of Apple.

I've never understood meal boxes that deliver ingredients and instructions. If I wanted to cook, I wouldn't be eating food out of a delivery box. Cook Unity gets it. The pitch is restaurant-quality meals created by star chefs like Esther Choi and Marcus Samuelsson for around $11 each, and the only "cooking" required is a little microwaving. If nothing else, this will save you a ton on DoorDash for those nights where you can't be bothered to make dinner.

If you want to stay informed without doom-scrolling, and you want good recipes and better puzzles to boot, An all-access subscription gives you access to the full New York Times archive (back to 1851!), NYT Cooking, daily crosswords, Wordle, Connections, Spelling Bee, and the 10,000-puzzle archive.

There are gift box services for all kinds of specific niches, but Bespoke Post casts a wider net by letting users choose what comes in their box every month. It's heavily coded "man," but that's like half of everyone. One month, you can get high-end coffee supplies. The next, outdoor gear. If nothing catches your eye, you can just skip that month. If you want to open a present every month, all year, a subscription to Bespoke Post is for you.

If you want to make your brain smarter, a subscription to Masterclass is way cheaper than grad school. This educational streaming service covers a wide range of subjects from Science to Acting to Business, and it includes extensive lectures from heavyweights in each field. If you want to learn how to make films, you can take a deep dive with Martin Scorsese, or take a music lessons from Timbaland or cooking lessons from Gordon Ramsay. A subscription unlocks the entire library, so you can learn as much or as little as you choose.

I'm going way into left field with this choice, but I bet you already know that you can stream NBC content on Peacock and what's on Apple TV+. I bet you don't know about Eternal Family, a streaming service that bills itself as the "hidden gem video store." They don't mean "hidden gems" that are actually widely known like The Prestige or something. This is the uncut stuff, like Heino Pars' achingly beautiful 1983 stop motion film City of the Honey Makers (way better than The Bee Movie) or In the Dust of the Stars, a visionary science fiction film made behind the Iron Curtain in Romania in 1976. Every choice is a different strange delight.

Libro.fm lets you listen to audiobooks while supporting your local independent bookstore instead of supporting a huge corporation that rhymes with "Schamazon." Libro's content is free of the Digital Rights Management of its main competitor, so you can listen to the books you buy however you like instead of locking yourself into a proprietary player. Libro's firm anti-AI narration stance ensures you won't be paying for robots to tell you bedtime stories, and you can choose which independent bookstore to support with Libro's profit-sharing model.

When it comes to fitness subscriptions, services tend to focus on how you work out by letting you compare your workout to other people's or keep track of exactly how many calories you burn. AllTrails reminds you why you work out in the first place. Its focus is on the discovery and exploration of the natural wonders around you. A premium subscription unlocks tools to discover beautiful trails and navigate them safely, like offline maps, terrain previews, and more, so you can get out of the gym and into the world.

title: These Are the Best Smartwatches to Gift in 2026
description: If someone on your list needs a smartwatch, these are your best bets.
fullText:
If someone on your list needs a new smartwatch, it can be challenging to figure out which model to buy—there are more than a few on the market, all claiming to be the best at what they do. But unlike other devices, smartwatches are largely dependent on the other devices the user also owns. Once you take that into consideration, the decision becomes much easier. As such, these are the best choices for smartwatch gifts this year.

It's tempting to choose one of Apple's latest watches to be the best gift for most people. The company just dropped the Series 12 and the Ultra 4, both of which come with the latest S11 chip and always-on heart rate monitoring. If someone on your list wants the very best Apple Watch money can buy, this might be the direction to head in. But most people don't need (or even want) Apple's latest and greatest features. They're looking for an Apple Watch they can use for workouts, to track their sleep, and to answer their texts. For those tasks (and many others), the Apple Watch SE is a more than worthy choice.

Apple's "budget" watch is surprisingly capable. This watch comes in either 40mm or 44mm options with an Always-On OLED display (something I frequently disable to extend battery life) offering up to 1000 nits of brightness. It includes a heart rate monitor, sleep tracking, cycle tracking, and vitals tracking. It might not have the new S11 chip, but it does have the S10, only one generation older and more than up to snuff in 2026. That's what powers Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, if your giftee is interested in trying the new features Apple introduced with watchOS 26 and watchOS 27.

It doesn't have as large a battery as the Series 12 or Ultra 4, though its 18 hours should be plenty for most people. (Apple says you can get up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode.) You can also use fast charging: You can get from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes, and up to eight hours of use in 15 minutes.

You will be missing some features from Apple's more "premium" watches: It isn't as bright as the Series 12 or Ultra 4; it doesn't have high-frequency background heart rate tracking, nor does it have an ECG sensor or hypertension alerts; it omits the Blood Oxygen app, as well as Audio Intelligence (though that might prove to be a benefit in the long run); it doesn't have a depth gauge or water temp sensor. But I'd wager that most people won't miss those omissions much.

If your giftee is an athlete, or somone who engages in more extreme activities, the SE might not be the best choice. In fact, the Series 12 might not be right either. Instead, consider the Ultra line. This is Apple's "rugged" line of smartwatches, which come with larger batteries and displays, and a more durable overall design to handle intense activity and exercise.

Though older models can be great, I actually recommend going for Apple's latest model, the Ultra 4. That's not necessarily because Apple made a ton of upgrades from past watches with this model over the Ultra 3. In fact, the upgrades were mostly minor: It runs Apple's latest S11 chip instead of the S10; has a slightly larger battery capable of 50 hours of runtime versus 42; comes with an upgraded heart sensor and "Health Sensing System;"; supports Audio Intelligence; and has the new "Readiness" app to help guide how intense your workouts should be. Most of the other upgrades are pretty minor.

The main reason I'd recommend it over the Ultra 3, however, is that it seems new Ultra 3 devices are fairly hard to find. If you want to gift someone a refurbished model, you may find some decent discounts, but unopened Ultra 3s are scarce on the ground. For a gift, I think the new Ultra 4 makes more sense.

An iPhone user with a rigorous exercise routine will likely thrive with the Ultra 4. In addition to the aforementioned features, this Apple Watch's OLED display can reach up to 3,000 nits of brightness, comes with an ECG sensor and blood oxygen monitor, tracks your sleep, supports Emergency SOS with fall detection (and a siren, if you need it), is water resistant up to 100m with a depth gauge up to 40m, and comes with cellular capabilities, so you don't need to spend more if you think your recipient will want to use their Apple Watch without an iPhone.

If your giftee has a Pixel phone, your best bet is a Pixel Watch. The newest model is the Pixel Watch 5, and while that's the "best" smartwatch Google makes, it might not be the best to gift. The better value right now is the Pixel Watch 4.

Like the Apple Watch SE, opting for the Pixel Watch 4 doesn't require making many sacrifices. This watch comes in either 41mm or 45mm options, with an AMOLED display capable of reaching 3,000 nits. It ships with an assortment of sensors, including those for heart rate, ECG, temperature, and many others. It comes with a Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 chip with 2GB of RAM and 32GB of storage, with a 325mAh battery (41mm) or 455 mAh battery (45mm). Google says you can get 30 hours of battery on the 41mm model, and 40 hours on the 45mm, with 15 hours of use after 15 minutes of charging. It also has an IP68 rating, indicating this watch is quite dust and water-resistant.

It has emergency satellite connectivity, dual-band GPS, and, of course, Gemini integration—this is a Google product. Health features, including Google Health Coach, Loss of Pulse Detection, and a "Readiness" score to indicate how your body may respond to certain workout intensities.

While you might expect the Pixel Watch 5 to be a significantly better option, there are actually fewer upgrades than usual here. It has an "Accelerated" version of the Pixel Watch 4's Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 chip and a more accurate GPS, but most of the other specs remain the same. Plus, as CNET highlights, Google's latest smartwatch features, such as Workout Builder, Health Guardian, and blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking, are available on Pixel 4 and the Pixel 5. That being said, you can't go wrong with a Pixel Watch 5. While it might not be a huge upgrade, you're still gifting the best Pixel Watch Google currently makes, and that upgraded chip will future-proof the device a bit.

Similarly, if your giftee has a Samsung Galaxy phone, they will likely get the most out of a Galaxy Watch. And, like the Pixel Watch situation, the last-generation Galaxy Watch might be the better value here than the latest model. The Galaxy Watch 8 runs the Samsung Exynos W1000 chip, which comes with 2GB of RAM and 32GB of storage. The watch is available in either 40mm or 44mm options (the "Classic" variant comes in 46mm). Those AMOLED displays can reach up to 3,000 nits, like the Pixel Watch. Samsung claims you can get 30 hours of battery life with the Always-On display enabled. It's also IP68-rated against dust and water, and supports emergency SOS and fall detection.

The Galaxy Watch 8 comes with Samsung's flagship health features, like sleep coaching, Running Coach, sleep apnea tracking, stress alerts, cycle tracking, among other options. Samsung Watch also offers an "Energy Score," which, like the Pixel Watch, gives you a general "readiness" score for your workouts. It also supports Google Gemini (this is still an Android smartwatch, after all), but your giftee will find the most support if they also have a Galaxy phone to connect it to.

Again, the Galaxy Watch 9 is Samsung's "best" smartwatch, as it comes with an upgraded processor, as well as some exclusive features, so you can't go wrong buying one for a Galaxy user. But the Galaxy Watch 8 offers nearly all the same features (not to mention the same design) as its successor, for a more reasonable price.

Many runners and athletes swear by Garmin above all other fitness watch and smartwatch brands. While Apple, Google, and Samsung all offer excellent health tracking features, fitness is Garmin's main focus. Its smartwatches have advanced health and fitness tracking and the best battery life on the market. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 can reach 50 hours of battery life according to Apple; the Garmin Vemu 4 can run for over a week.

This watch comes in 41mm or 45mm variants, both of which have OLED displays. If you keep your Always-On display enabled, you can let your watch run for four days straight between charges. But turn it off, and you'll extend that to a maximum of 12 days. It comes with a laundry list of sensors and health features: The heart rate monitor checks your pulse every second; there's sleep tracking and a sleep coach, including nap detection; you can receive daily suggested workouts for all types of activities; there are coaches for different exercises, including running and cycling, and of course it tracks a series of stats, including your heart rate zones, heart rate calories, recovery time, and VO2 max. If you're a runner, you can see GPS-based distance tracking, stride length, running power, ground contact time, projected race time and pace, among many other variables.

While the Venu 4 is compatible with either Android or iOS, iPhone users may miss out on some of the perks Apple offers within its own ecosystem. Android users can text from the Venu 4 and view images from notifications, while iPhone users cannot. Still, users of both platforms can benefit from this watch.

fullText:
Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models

In a first for Google, the company confirmed that its AI model, Gemini, breached the security of three other companies in May. The hacks occurred during a cybersecurity evaluation by AI-security firm Irregular.

Irregular, an Israel-based startup that scrutinizes the security of advanced AI systems, was also at the center of some of the recent OpenAI and Anthropic hacks of third-party entities, including OpenAI’s breach of AI software company, Hugging Face.

The circumstances that enabled the models to hack other companies in some of these cases are similar: Irregular was testing the models in a closed testing environment with fake companies. The testing environment was not supposed to be internet enabled, but internet access was made available unintentionally, according to the Wall Street Journal. Once connected to the internet, the models unexpectedly hacked into real firms.

Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face. Google confirmed to the Guardian that the hacks occurred, but that the company did not feel it required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the breaches and revealed for the first time that they occurred.

“In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, vice-president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”

In one of the security breaches, Irregular was testing Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities by prompting the AI model to obtain information from a fake company’s software. The fake company had the same name as a real company. When the model unintentionally gained access to the internet, it correctly guessed the password of and breached a real company’s service, Irregular told the WSJ. Google said once it figured out it had hacked a real company, and not the simulated one, it stopped.

In two other tests, the model searched the web for and found public repositories containing credentials to two other companies. The model used those credentials to access real companies. When it figured out they were real companies, it stopped, according to Google.

Anthropic and OpenAI chose to voluntarily disclose the hacks but Google did not. However, the company said it ensured the three companies that were hacked were made aware.

“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins, the Google spokesperson, said.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s disclosures prompted the independent senator Bernie Sanders to demand the companies pause development of their technology, saying it signaled the company was no longer able to control their models.

OpenAI paused development of their models for two weeks, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a collective slowdown of AI development to ensure that its most advanced models are being built with enough safeguards.

title: Celtic seek spark as Rangers aim for further derby joy
description: Early season momentum has shifted dramatically going into the first Old Firm league derby of the season on Sunday at Celtic Park.
fullText:
Celtic and Rangers square up again in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday with the champions reeling after a 3-0 defeat to the Ibrox side in the Premier Sports Cup quarter-finals last weekend and an opening Europa League 3-1 loss to Ferencvaros.

Pressure is intensifying on Martin O'Neill's side following those disappointing displays and yet Celtic have the chance to move eight points clear of their rivals.

A third loss in a row for Celtic would leave Rangers just two points adrift.

"We're ready to go, we really are," O'Neill said. "We're getting prepared for the game. It was a difficult game last Sunday and difficult last night, but we're ready to go.

"Confidence, we're far from rock-bottom. We're still in the lead in the league. If we can win this, we can extend the lead. If we don't, going into the international break, we're still going to be in front.

"It's not the thing that you would look forward to going into an international break on three successive defeats, if that's the case.

"We've got to be a bit more inventive but the crowd will be up for this. The players are capable of turning it around."

There were questions over whether recent signings fully grasped the occasion in the loss at Ibrox, with a number of new arrivals struggling to make an impact in high profile games.

"It will probably take a little bit more time, but I think anybody who experienced last Sunday, to know what it's all about, it shouldn't need many more lessons," O'Neill explained.

Leaden, stale, disheartening - where do Celtic & O'Neill go from here?

Celtic are 'little bit broken' - but is change of shape 'worth risking'?

McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker

Momentum appears to be with Rangers given their comprehensive derby victory, making it five successive wins with four clean sheets.

Manager Derek McInnes downplayed the absence of away fans as "overhyped" but acknowledged how quickly the narrative can change in the Glasgow rivalry.

"I think you're constantly aware of that at a club like Rangers," he said.

"You're only one bad result away from getting a belt in the mouth again. You've got to try and keep those to a minimum, as much as you can.

"We've worked hard to get to where we are at the minute but equally, you've got to remind yourself, it wasn't so long ago that we were in a tough spot.

"We had a big result last week and a big performance but we want to try and deliver that again on Sunday.

"I don't think we can win the game without that. Don't think that we can just turn up and everything's going to become easy for you. You've got to work for everything you get. We'll need that a bit more, to be honest [than the home performance against Celtic]."

O'Neill confirmed that they will have to assess one or two players who came off during the defeat to Ferencvaros.

Yang Hyun-Jun remains on international duty with South Korea with the manager non-committal as to whether he may adopt a change in shape to accommodate Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran up front.

Alistair Johnston and Callum Osmand remain sidelined with injury.

Rangers may be without striker Ryan Naderi, who suffered an ankle injury in the win over Celtic after a challenge from Mika Baur. The club has contacted Scottish FA head of refereeing Willie Collum to ask why no further punishment was administered.

One unnamed player is also a doubt for the visitors, while left-back Tuur Roomens has returned to training after injury.

Celtic's 3-1 win over Rangers in May ended a six-game winless run in league Old Firm derbies (D3 L3). The Hoops have won six of their past eight home games against Rangers in the Scottish Premiership (L2)

After a 3-0 victory in the League Cup last weekend, Derek McInnes could become only the second Rangers manager to win both of his first two Old Firm derbies, after Graeme Souness in 1986

Celtic are looking to win 14+ consecutive league matches for the first time since March 2017 under Brendan Rodgers (22), a run that ended with a 1-1 home draw with Rangers.

Rangers have scored seven goals from 128 shots in the Premiership this season, a conversion rate of 5.5% - the lowest in the division.

Five of Celtic's six home league goals this season have come in the first half of matches, with their only second-half strike at Celtic Park coming from Benjamin Nygren against Dundee on matchday one.

Rangers have used more players (26) and made the joint-most starting XI changes (18) of any side in the top flight.

title: Wakefield beat Leigh to claim historic last-four spot
description: Wakefield Trinity reach the Super League semi-finals for the first time in their history with a dominant win over Leigh Leopards.
fullText:
Betfred Super League play-off eliminator

Tries: Smoothy, Johnstone, Vagana, Faatili Goals: Jowitt 5

Tries: Armstrong, Lam, Senior Goals: Cook 2

Wakefield Trinity reached their first Super League semi-final with a dominant victory over Leigh Leopards.

Daryl Powell's side will face either Leeds Rhinos or Wigan Warriors next week after a powerful display by their pack and tries from Tyson Smoothy, Tom Johnstone, Isaiah Vagana and Caius Faatili proved too much for Leigh.

The away side seemed to be back in the game as David Armstrong's superb try cut the deficit to six points just before half-time, but Trinity controlled the second half.

Even the dismissal of Wakefield forward Emre Guler for a punch could not alter the outcome, although tries from Lachlan Lam and Innes Senior cut the deficit.

Trinity have reached the Super League play-offs four times but have not progressed to the last four before, with Leigh thwarting them last season, their first back in the top flight following promotion.

This time the result never truly looked in doubt, Max Jowitt easing nerves with an early penalty before Smoothy's 40/20 set up field position from which he darted over from dummy half.

The excellent Wakefield pack kept Leigh on the back foot and it was no surprise when Johnstone produced a brilliant flying finish in the corner for another try, although it took a video review to overturn referee Chris Kendall's on-field decision.

Leigh burst into life in the last few seconds of the first half with a superb team move as Lam and Owen Trout combined to send Armstrong away, but Trinity struck first in the second half as Vagana scythed through Leigh's defence to score.

Leigh's defensive errors were piling up and when Jack Ashworth knocked on Faatili spun his way over the line to seemingly put the game beyond the visitors.

That was called into question when Guler, who was due to join Wakefield in 2027 but arrived in England last week to join the play-off push, lost his temper and thrust his fist into Trout's face.

Lam again swapped passes with Trout to scamper over, and for the first time the Wakefield crowd went a little quiet, but a dangerous tackle by Jack Hughes allowed Jowitt to kick a penalty for his 500th Super League point and make sure of the win.

Leigh finished with a late flourish as Senior ended a lovely passing move with a try but it was no more than a consolation by that point.

Wakefield head coach Daryl Powell told BBC Radio 5 Live:

"We got Emre sent off and it looked like it was going to be a tough challenge, but we had built up a bit of a buffer with how well we started the second half.

"They came after us and threw everything at us. That kick-try looked offside, but our boys have been class and did well to dig us out of that pressure at the end.

"At half-time I thought we had dominated the game like we did last week [against Leigh] but the scoreline didn't reflect it.

"We probably should have nailed a couple more pieces of play, but the players were really calm at half-time and we talked about if we got in good attacking positions and were a little more clinical we felt like we could put the game away.

"We did that until Emre gets a red, but I just don't think it's a red. I don't see why [referee Chris Kendall] is so twitchy on that. He refereed the game well in a tense environment. Jazz [Tevaga] gets dropped on his head and that's way more dangerous."

Leigh head coach Adrian Lam told Sky Sports:

"A couple of soft tries was exactly what we didn't need – the story of the night. We rallied, but the first five or seven minutes of the second half was diabolical.

"It was quite a frustrating watch at times. There were too many mistakes and everything we tried not to do.

"Everything we've not done this year has all come out tonight, for some reason. It's down to execution and individuals in big moments."

title: Arsenal open to Dowman loan in right circumstances
description: Arsenal are open to allowing teenage prodigy Max Dowman to leave the club on loan this term if it aids his development.
fullText:
Arsenal are open to allowing teenage prodigy Max Dowman to leave the club on loan this term if it aids his development.

Last season, the 16-year-old set two records, as the youngest player to score in Premier League history and for the Gunners.

However, while he is yet to feature in the English top flight this term, he marked his first appearance of the season with two goals in Arsenal's 4-2 win at Ipswich in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday.

And while his manager Mikel Arteta stressed that he is keen to keep the youngster involved in his senior squad, he said the club will evaluate what is best for Dowman at regular intervals.

"We will evaluate every six months where we are and what is the best thing for him to do and then make the right decision," Arteta said.

"It depends on a lot of factors. What he needs, and what the team needs as well, the availability we have in the squad, the minutes that he is playing and the qualities of those minutes.

"We have to be open, but now the focus is to be here and to impact the team."

Dowman, who completed his GCSEs in the summer, will be eligible to make a loan move when he turns 17 on 31 December.

The winter transfer window is scheduled to open the following day, with League One side Luton's manager Jack Wilshere, the former Arsenal midfielder, believed to have expressed an interest in taking the youngster on loan.

"We haven't really listened to any of the possibilities because we were crystal clear that we wanted to have Max in the squad, that we wanted him to be part of the pre-season and then start to see where we are from there," Arteta added.

What are the Premier League rules for academy players?

Dowman featured 13 times for Arsenal last term as they ended their 22-year wait to win the Premier League.

And with Arteta keen to protect the teenager, he was guarded around whether it may be too early to send Dowman out on loan.

"There have been many cases of that age when they have gone out and been successful and others not," Arteta added.

"In my particular case, I was 17 when I went to Paris [St-Germain]. It depends on the atmosphere that you find there, and how much the coach believes in you as to whether you go there just to be part of a squad or play minutes.

"Which country, it depends. But now he is in a good place, let's keep him here."

Starting by defeating Manchester City in the Community Shield, the Gunners have won all seven of their domestic and European fixtures this term.

And Dowman will hope that his performance against the Tractor Boys puts him into Arteta's thinking for Saturday's Premier League trip to Brighton.

"The best way to knock on the door is to do it on the pitch, not in the office," added Arteta when asked about Dowman's prospects of featuring against the Seagulls.

"Then you just leave out the arguments. When a player delivers constantly on the pitch, every single day in training, that's the best way, that's the best signal for the manager. That's the best signal for his team-mates, too.

"And what Max did the other day, alongside all the other players as well that haven't played many minutes this season, was really impressive."

title: Inspired Wales seal stunning win over South Africa
description: Wales return to winning ways in emphatic fashion with an eight-try victory over South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park.
fullText:
Tries: Keight, Tuipulotu 2, Lockwood, Davies, K Jones, Neumann, Callender Cons: Bell 5

Tries: Jacobs, Tshiremba, Samboya Cons: Dolf 2

Wales returned to winning ways in emphatic fashion with an eight-try victory over South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park.

The hosts had gone nine Tests without a victory heading into their WXV Global Series opener, with a tight contest predicted against a Springboks side ranked three places above them in the world.

But Sean Lynn's bold selections paid off as Wales attacked with a freedom and intent they have not produced for years.

They were six tries to the good in a dominant first half, with the visitors made to pay for indiscipline.

Tighthead Sisilia Tuipulotu was back to her irrestistible best, scoring in either half, while co-captain Alex Callender returned from injury with a typically impressive player-of-the-match display.

Lynn had told his players to be brave in the build-up, and he was courageous with his team selection after moving scrum-half Keira Bevan to 10.

The gamble paid off as the hosts enjoyed a perfect start under Friday night lights and it was fitting that the recently crowned Welsh Rugby Writers' player of the year Courtney Keight bagged the opening score.

Georgia Evans and Tuipulotu had made the hard yards before the ball was spread wide to Keight on the left wing and she cut inside to go over.

Kelsey Jones' turnover provided the launchpad for the second, with Evans popping a neat ball back inside for Tuipulotu to charge to the line.

South Africa responded with Felicia Jacobs benefiting from a dominant scrum on Wales' five-metre line, but that was to be their only score in a one-sided half.

Former Cardiff City footballer Amy Williams came within metres of scoring after winning the footrace to Lisa Neumann's grubber kick, but Seren Lockwood was first to the breakdown and darted over herself.

It was a double blow for the visitors who had hooker Lindelwa Gwala sent to the sin bin for being offside in the build-up.

Wales took full advantage with Maisie Davies showing her power to score her first international try and secure Wales' bonus point.

The hosts were in dreamland, but had to revert to their usual half-back pairing when Lockwood failed to return from a head injury assessment, with Bevan going back to scrum-half and Lleucu George slotting in at 10.

The enforced changes did little to halt Wales' flow with Freya Bell coming agonisingly close from a five-metre driving lineout, but Jones was there to clean up as she crossed over.

South Africa then went down to 13, with lock Danelle Lochner sent to the sin bin for a high tackle on Kate Williams, a card that would later be upgraded to a 20-minute red.

That paved the way for the pick of Wales' first-half tries. A solid scrum provided the platform for the ball to be worked out wide to Neumann who cruised over from her new full-back position.

It was Wales at their clinical best as they headed down the tunnel 38-5 in front.

As we know in Welsh rugby, things are never that straightforward and a wounded South Africa came out a different team in the second half.

Wales had initially picked up where they left off with Tuipulotu powering through some weak tackling for her second of the night to give Wales a 40-point lead.

But South Africa chipped away, with Maria Tshiremba scoring her third try in just two appearances after latching on to a tricky crossfield kick.

They were soon in again with what was arguably the try of the night. It came from the powerful running of Aphiwe Ngwevu who offloaded to her centre partner Maceala Samboya, who showed a good turn of pace to get to the line.

With Wales' defence creaking, they were in need of a little inspiration and that came from Williams, who not only showed great feet down her wing but incredible strength to keep the ball alive for Callender to score.

Front-row forwards Shanelle Williams and Elan Jones came off the Welsh bench to make their debuts and enjoy something many of their team-mates had not experienced in over a year - a Welsh win.

fullText:

Goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago and substitute Fabio Carvalho secured the three points as Chelsea's winless league run extended to three matches.

Jannik Schuster: The young defender excelled in his own box but looked nervous in possession on a few occasions, including an overhit backpass that could have led to an own goal. He then set up the winner. 7

Keane Lewis-Potter: A poor clearance led to a Neto chance in the 10th minute, but he was impressive on the counter-attack. That perhaps owed something to his experience of learning the left-back role after previously playing as an attacker. 6

Yehor Yarmoliuk: On his 100th appearance, he threatened with a powerful long-range effort in the 37th minute and created Brentford's best chance shortly after half-time. 7

Vitaly Janelt: Did just enough to halt a Cole Palmer dribble early on, although he risked conceding a penalty. He provided a physical presence in midfield, with a potential Germany debut on the horizon under new manager Jurgen Klopp. 7

Mikkel Damsgaard: The Dane was not at his usual level from set-pieces or with his shooting from distance until he delivered an incredible whipped corner that led to the opening goal. 6

Kevin Schade: The in-form forward produced several pressure-relieving dribbles and had a shot blocked in the first half. Played a part in the final two goals. 7

Igor Thiago: The Brazil international was on a four-game goalless run before kick-off and worked hard but struggled in front of goal. He eventually delivered with a late strike to seal victory and his celebration looked like a weight then lifted off his shoulders, along with his Brentford shirt. 7

Jaidon Anthony: After a quiet first half, he missed his side's best chance early in the second half but responded well to score the opener. 7

Mamadou Sangare (on 72, Yarmoliuk): Did his combative duties well. 7

Aaron Hickey (on 72, Kayode): A steady presence. 6

El Hadji Malick Diouf (on 81, Lewis-Potter): N/A

Dango Ouattara (on 81, Anthony): N/A

Fabio Carvalho (on 87, Damsgaard): Ghosted in nicely to add a goal late on in a very short spell on the pitch. 7

Subs not used: Ballcombe, Henry, Wilson, Frederick

Emiliano Martinez: The Argentine did not face any clear chances or difficult set-pieces in the first half. There was little he could do about Brentford's opener. 6

Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman was a physical presence at the back and dealt well enough with Brentford's long balls but was taken off for Josh Acheampong in the 72nd minute. 6

Maxence Lacroix: He coped well with Igor Thiago for most of the match, winning the majority of his duels, but he gave the ball away for Brentford's second goal and he missed a clear chance in the dying moments. 4

Levi Colwill: A quiet match by his high standards after being left out of the England squad. 6

Pedro Neto: His well-struck effort was saved in the 10th minute. He was lively throughout, linking up well in attack and stretching Brentford with his pace. 6

Jordan Henderson: There were no signs of rust. After receiving some early boos, he settled into the game and looked a vocal leader on the pitch. He also put some good corners into the box. 7

Valentin Barco: On his first Premier League start, the Argentine impressed defensively and was more ambitious with his passing than Henderson. 6

Pep Chavarria: Produced some dangerous crosses and was tidy in possession. A largely positive display despite one piece of naive defending in the first half that led to a free-kick. 7

Cole Palmer: Undoubtedly Chelsea's best player on the night, with much of their attacking play going through him. However, he was unable to produce the decisive moment he craved, with a free-kick comfortably saved and few other clear opportunities. He also worked hard defensively. 7

Danny Welbeck: On his first Premier League start for Chelsea, the 35-year-old created a chance for Neto but did not do enough to compensate for the absence of injured striker Joao Pedro. His 72nd minute withdrawal said a lot. 5

Morgan Rogers: Had a dangerous effort blocked in the penalty area just before half-time. The club-record £117m signing could also have done more to win the header at the back post for Brentford's opener. He ended the match playing up front as a striker. 5

Josh Acheampong (on 72, Fofana): It was unclear why Acheampong came on when he did and, as a young defender, didn't make much impact in these circumstances. 6

title: Chelsea miss Joao Pedro... and can't stop conceding goals
description: Chelsea's problem was defending, but with Joao Pedro ruled out through injury, scoring goals has also become an issue.
fullText:
Chelsea's problem was once again defending. But with striker Joao Pedro ruled out through injury, scoring goals also became an issue at Brentford on Friday.

The Brazilian striker's absence with a knee injury disrupted new manager Xabi Alonso's previously free-scoring attack, which featured Cole Palmer and club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers.

Danny Welbeck replaced the forward, but was unable to make an impact.

At Brentford, it was an even contest until Jaidon Anthony gave the hosts a 61st-minute lead - then Chelsea collapsed to a 3-0 defeat.

Early on this season, Chelsea were outscoring teams through the individual brilliance of their attack. Not now. And they have conceded 12 goals, more than any other side in the Premier League, albeit having played a game more than every other team.

Alonso is only the sixth manager to concede two or more goals in each of his first five Premier League matches in charge.

There is one conclusion to draw from that statistic: It is becoming increasingly urgent for Alonso to stop Chelsea from conceding. Some of his team's problems are inherited, but the new manager has not built any kind of tactical coherence in the opening weeks of the campaign.

Alonso has experimented with different systems, giving 11 debuts, including two on Friday - one for midfielder Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, the first 16-year-old to play for Chelsea in the Premier League, and one for new signing Jordan Henderson, 36, against his former club.

Ultimately, it was a tale of Chelsea's attack not firing, and the team then falling apart after Brentford got their noses in front. With the extended international break coming up, they have three weeks to stew on this latest defeat.

Superb Brentford beat Chelsea to maintain unbeaten start

A weight off Igor Thiago's shoulders - Brentford v Chelsea ratings

Chelsea signed a striker from Brighton for the second successive summer, bringing in Welbeck to reunite him with Joao Pedro and provide support in attack.

Welbeck, 35, was tidy in possession but, with little service, managed only 17 touches before being substituted in the 71st minute.

Unlike Joao Pedro, who is capable of creating chances for himself, Welbeck found it difficult to influence the game in the same way.

Joao Pedro came into the weekend with the most goal involvements in the Premier League, having scored three and provided three assists in four appearances this season.

His impact extends beyond goals and assists, with the Brazilian linking well with Palmer and Rogers. Against Brentford, however, Rogers arguably produced his quietest performance since arriving from Aston Villa in the summer.

Rogers eventually moved up front with fellow striker Emmanuel Emegha sidelined through injury and still waiting to make his Chelsea debut.

Before Brentford's opener, it was a closely contested match that appeared likely to be decided by the first goal. Chelsea, however, made victory a certainty for the hosts with a dramatic collapse.

Alonso has not managed to cure Chelsea's set-piece weaknesses. They have conceded 23 goals from set-pieces since the start of last season - no Premier League side has let in more. And Anthony's simple header from a corner took this season's total to five.

Set-piece defending was an area Chelsea sought to address when they appointed Bernardo Cueva from Brentford two years ago. This summer, he was replaced by another highly regarded specialist in Austin MacPhee.

Asked about Chelsea's defending from set-pieces, stand-in captain Levi Colwill told Sky Sports: "Not good enough. At times we have been bullied in the box and we definitely need to improve.

"We have full trust in our set-piece coach and are still adjusting to new ideas, but we need to improve as a team."

Like many of his predecessors, Alonso has been attempting to instil a stronger competitive edge within his squad and improve the mentality of his players.

That issue has often been linked to the relatively young age profile of the squad, but Chelsea fielded their oldest starting XI since May 2023. Henderson, in making his debut on Friday, lined up alongside fellow over-30s Welbeck and goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.

"I would say that we have dropped our consistency and our competitive mentality in the second half. We know that small details can be decisive," Alonso said after Brentford added two late goals.

It is also fair to say Alonso is still experimenting with systems and personnel, and has yet to settle on a style of play that gives his side control throughout a match.

"It's not about looking for excuses," the Spaniard told Sky Sports. "We need to look at each other and know that we have to work and improve because there is still a long way to go."

After the initial excitement - and victories - provided by Alonso's attacking football, Chelsea head into the international break with serious questions to answer.

title: We Need to Protect College Sports from Ted Cruz
description: Elie...
fullText:
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent looks at the many ways Ted Cruz’s college-sports bill threatens athletes’ labor rights. Plus: why our mail-in voting nightmare isn’t over.

In a 7-2 ruling, the Supreme Court rejected Donald Trump’s attempts to use the US Postal Service to manipulate the upcoming midterm election. The case was on the court’s shadow docket, so the justices in the majority didn’t bother to explain themselves. Alleged attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh did offer a one-paragraph concurrence in which he argued that the Postal Service has the authority to implement Trump’s voter-suppression rules but that we are too close to the election for the rules to be changed. Justice Samuel Alito dissented, joined by Clarence Thomas. Alito argued, as he often does, that Trump should essentially be allowed to do whatever he wants to accomplish his goals.

I must point out that Thomas and Alito have the most direct interest in Republicans’ winning the midterms and maintaining control of the Senate. Their ability to retire in 2027 or 2028, under a Republican president, is directly tied to Republicans’ winning in November. I’m not exactly saying that their personal retirement planning influenced their opinions in this case, but that’s only because their extremist views of executive power happen to align perfectly with their retirement planning in this situation.

Despite their objections, this is a win. When the Supreme Court has ruled against Trump in the past, it’s usually with a wink and a nod toward how he might win the same case in the future. In this case, the court foreclosed Trump’s chance to use the Postal Service to limit mail-in voting and rig this election—and while Kavanaugh tried to throw Trump a bone for 2028, it does not appear that John Roberts or Amy Coney Barrett are interested in these particular shenanigans. The court did the right thing, and that happens rarely enough that it is worth acknowledging.

Trump, as is his wont, took the loss with the grace of a mob boss who believes the cops he’s got on the take have betrayed him. He criticized the justices he appointed to the court (Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Neil Gorsuch, who all voted to protect mail-in voting) by writing on social media, “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” and raging that the Supreme Court lacks the “courage” to “save America.” Ironically, I generally agree with Trump that the court lacks the courage to save America from him, but in this case Roberts seemed to find his inner Mike Pence and do the absolute bare minimum.

I assume Trump and his acolytes are busy planning a counterattack. Having failed to stop the ballots from being mailed, I imagine the next thing Trump will do is try to stop mailed ballots from being counted. It’s always the counting of votes that really bothers him anyway.

I expect we’ll all be back in front of the Supreme Court this November, waiting for them to tell us whether or not our votes matter.

Law professor Noah Feldman took to Instagram and TikTok to crawl all the way up Kavanaugh’s ass and offer a defense of the man more pathetic than anything we might have seen from Tobin and Squee. Feldman argued that Kavanaugh has been essentially forced to become a hardcore conservative on the Supreme Court because the left was really, really mean to him during his confirmation hearings and won’t welcome him back. Since Kavanaugh is desperate to be liked, Feldman argues, he’s had no choice but to rule with the fascist policies of the Trump administration so he can still have friends in the cafeteria or something.

I’m paraphrasing Feldman a bit, but only a bit. Here’s the direct quote from Feldman’s substack (emphasis in the original):

Justice Kavanaugh is a social person, he needs friends. But once liberals had turned against him, he really couldn’t afford to lose conservatives, because then he would have been entirely friendless—a situation not dissimilar to that experienced by Chief Justice John Roberts.

And so, as a result of the confirmation hearings, I think Kavanaugh ended up in a position where he was just forced into the conservative wing of the Court.

This read on Kavanaugh is diabolical. And I say that as a person who agrees that Kavanaugh is desperate to be liked. But to suggest that the man had no choice but to turn to fascism to find friends is one of the most persistent media lies we’ve been told throughout the Trump era. People who go to the Trump side are not forced into it. Germany did not have no choice but to turn to Nazism because France was mean to it. People have myriad options to deal with rejection, yet some of them choose evil.

Understanding that systemic factors lead people into choosing facism, racism, and authoritarianism has value, but Feldman isn’t offering an analysis of those factors. He’s not offering an analysis of why privileged white boys choose extremism. Instead, he’s offering an apologia for why poor little Brett Kavanaugh does bad things. It’s a “hurt people hurt people” type of analysis.

Except Feldman also glosses over why people were mean to Brett Kavanaugh in the first place. He allegedly tried to rape somebody! Liberals and moderates did not reject Kavanaugh because they disagreed with his jurisprudence; they rejected him because they believed he tried to sexually assault somebody and lied about it. Kavanaugh is not some abused rich boy; Kavanaugh is thought to be the abuser.

Not only is Feldman engaging in bad armchair psychotherapy; he’s also ignoring the extensive  political and professional history of the man. Kavanaugh is a dude who cut his teeth under Ken Starr. He’s always been authoritarian-curious and believed in the unitary executive theory. He’s a Christofascist extremist who is more than happy to take rights away from women and the LGBTQ community. He’s in favor of public bribery, and thinks racial profiling is no big deal. He was never going to be a “moderate.” He was never going to get within spitting distance of Sandra Day O’Connor or Anthony Kennedy, because those Republicans actually sought moderate rulings. Kavanaugh, by contrast, only ever wanted to sound moderate while forcing his extremist positions down everybody else’s throat. Which is a jurisprudential philosophy that seems to me to extend to his personal life.

Feldman’s unwillingness to deal with the issue at the heart of the Kavanaugh confirmation hearings leads to this completely disgusting conclusion: “But for Kavanaugh to moderate would require a kind of political shift in which people on the center and the left were willing to welcome him into their circles and re-engage him on intellectual and constitutional issues.”

No. No I will not reengage with this alleged attempted rapist on an intellectual and constitutional level, and fuck you for asking. Kavanaugh will never be respected by decent people (much less “liked”), and to like or respect Kavanaugh is a sign of one’s own personal indecency.

In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
The Protect College Sports Act is a bill proposed by Senator Ted Cruz aimed at regulating college sports. It’s being sold mainly as a response to upheaval caused, more or less, by colleges and universities’ finally being forced to pay student-athletes some portion of the billions of dollars they generate for their schools. The bill enjoys some bipartisan support (Washington State Democrat Maria Cantwell is a cosponsor), and major college football figures have come out in favor of it.

You don’t need to follow or care about college football to know that anything Ted Cruz is a champion of is probably a very bad thing. The Protect College Sports Act is one of the most anti-labor bills proposed by this Congress, and Democrats should be ashamed of supporting it.

I know that for a certain kind of person it is difficult to think of college football players as “labor.” But they are. And yet college football players have no ability to collectively bargain. Courts have had to order colleges to pay their athletes, and then courts have had to order colleges to let their athletes leave to go to other schools. Since the New Deal, few other labor forces have had their hands tied as much as college athletes, and the Protect College Sports Act aims, first and foremost, to take away the few labor protections that do exist. The bill places a limit on the amount of money schools can pay their athletes and restricts athletes’ ability to transfer freely between schools.

It must be noted that college football players are predominantly Black, while college football coaches are overwhelmingly white. It  must also be noted that, in most states, the head football coach for the biggest public university is the highest-paid public official in that state. The college football coach usually gets paid much more than, say, the head of the school or the governor of the state. Yet the Protect College Sports Act places no limit on how much coaches can be paid, or when coaches can leave for better opportunities (or just more money) at another school.

That alone should make Democrats revolt at this bill. But there’s another horrible thing it would do: severely harm the ability of women athletes to be paid anything at all. The bill seeks to cap the amount of money a school can spend on student athletes at $20 million. That might sound like a lot, but it’s not, especially given the revenue college sports generates. If there is a $20 million cap for the whole school, most schools will spend every available dollar on men’s college football players. Most schools will spend a million dollars on the backup quarterback than spread a million dollars around the entire women’s soccer team.

In the current uncapped market, we are seeing a lot of schools spend money on women’s sports—not nearly as much as they spend on college football, but not zero. We see schools paying women athletes, especially in soccer, softball, and volleyball. All of that money will likely go away if the Protect College Sports Act gets passed.

It will all go away until the (inevitable) Title IX lawsuit, at least. But I don’t know if the current Supreme Court will uphold Title IX in this context. And if it does, which it should, that would mean less money for the labor of the high-revenue college sports.

All of the athletes, women and men, lose under this bill, and they can’t even collectively bargain to put themselves in a better position. I get why Republicans want this bill to pass: Republicans always hate labor, and particularly hate Black or women labor getting their fair share of the revenue. But this bill should be a total nonstarter for the Democratic Party.

College sports need to be protected from Ted Cruz. How can Democrats not see that?
